title: Design a Web Crawler
relevance: High — canonical 45-min HLD (Alex Xu Vol.1 ch.9); FAANG + Indian product cos (Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft); probes pipelines, politeness, dedup, and scheduling more than a public REST API.
company_notes: Campus/new-grad: seed→frontier→fetch→parse with robots + basic dedup; Bloom and Mercator queues differentiate. Experienced/FAANG (1–5+ YOE): same prompt with deep probes on two-tier frontier, host sharding, DNS, retry/DLQ, content dedup, traps, and re-crawl scheduling. Top-tier canonical HLD (with URL shortener, rate limiter, chat, news feed, YouTube); in ByteByteGo Vol.1, Hello Interview, and system-design-primer.

phases.goal: Scope crawl+store vs search/LLM training, lock functional/non-functional needs, and state scale framing aloud.

must_hit.point: Functional in-scope: seed URLs, fetch HTML, extract text and links, store content, discover new URLs, respect robots.txt, avoid duplicate URL work.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists seed→fetch→extract→store→discover with robots and URL dedup as must-haves.

must_hit.point: Park out of scope unless asked: training the LLM / building search ranker, images/video, JS-rendered SPAs, authenticated pages.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explicitly parks indexing/ranking, media, headless JS, and login walls.

must_hit.point: Non-functional: politeness, fault tolerance (resume without losing frontier), scalability to billions of pages, robustness to bad HTML, traps, and timeouts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names politeness, resumable frontier, billion-page scale, and trap/timeout robustness.

must_hit.point: Pick a framing and state assumptions — e.g. Hello Interview ~10B pages, ~2 MB/page, finish in ~5 days; or primer ~1B links with weekly refresh.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States one concrete framing with those page/size/time assumptions out loud.

probes: What are we building — a crawler that stores pages, or a full search engine?
What stays out of scope unless I pull you there?

hints.1: Start by listing what the crawler must do versus what search/LLM systems do downstream.
hints.2: Separate functional (seed, fetch, parse, store, robots, dedup) from non-functional (politeness, resume, scale, traps).
hints.3: Say: crawl+store in; indexing/ranking parked; pick ~10B pages / ~5 days or primer ~1B links and stick to it.

phases.goal: Derive order-of-magnitude throughput, bandwidth, and storage, and explain why many hosts × low per-host QPS still scales.

must_hit.point: Throughput: 10B pages / 5 days ≈ ~23k pages/s average (order-of-magnitude; peak higher).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States ~23k pages/s from 10B over 5 days as average OM.

must_hit.point: Bandwidth: 23k × 2 MB ≈ tens of GB/s aggregate — drives fleet size and NIC class, not API QPS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties aggregate tens of GB/s to fleet/NICs rather than public API QPS.

must_hit.point: Storage: 10B × (HTML or extracted text) → multi-PB; compression and content dedup matter.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls multi-PB storage and why compression/content dedup help.

must_hit.point: Insight: per-host ~1 req/s still yields huge global QPS because you crawl many hosts in parallel.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains global QPS comes from host parallelism, not raising per-host rate.

probes: Walk me through back-of-envelope for pages/s, bandwidth, and storage.
How do you get high global throughput if you only do about one request per host per second?

hints.1: Use the framing numbers you already stated (pages, days, size per page).
hints.2: Compute pages/s, then bandwidth, then storage order of magnitude; call out parallel hosts.
hints.3: Say ~23k pages/s, tens of GB/s, multi-PB, and many hosts × ~1 req/s.

phases.goal: Clarify this is an internal pipeline with a thin control plane, not a public product API.

must_hit.point: Crawler is mostly an internal pipeline; sketch control-plane ops, not a public product API.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says data pipeline + control plane; not a user-facing REST product.

must_hit.point: POST /seeds submits seed URL list with priority and max_depth; GET status/counts for crawled, queued, failed.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions seed submit and status/count endpoints.

must_hit.point: Workers pull next URL from frontier (or consume queue), write blobs, ack on success; DLQ after N fetch failures; optional POST recrawl.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes worker pull/ack, DLQ on repeated fetch failures, optional force refresh.

probes: Where is the API for this system?
How do operators seed a crawl and see progress?

hints.1: Ask whether they expect a public API or an internal control plane.
hints.2: Sketch seeds, status, optional recrawl; workers consume frontier/queues.
hints.3: POST /seeds, GET /status, worker pull+ack+DLQ; clarify pipeline not product API.

phases.goal: Model URL/host metadata, seen-sets, blob keys, and where frontier/scheduling state lives.

must_hit.point: Url record: url_id, canonical_url, host, status (queued|fetched|parsed|skipped|failed), depth, priority, content_hash, html/text blob keys, last_crawled_at, next_fetch_at, http_status.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists canonical URL fields including status, depth, priority, hashes, blob keys, and fetch times.

must_hit.point: Host record caches robots_txt, crawl_delay_s, last_fetch_at, robots_fetched_at for politeness.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Has a Host entity holding robots cache and crawl-delay/last-fetch timing.

must_hit.point: SeenUrl / Bloom of canonical URL hashes; optional SeenContent / Bloom or indexed content hashes; blobs like raw/{url_id}.html.gz and text/{url_id}.txt.gz.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates URL-seen and content-seen from object-store blob keys.

must_hit.point: Metadata in Dynamo/Cassandra/Postgres sharded by url_id or host; frontier via Redis/SQS/Kafka plus per-host scheduling state.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Places metadata store and frontier/queue tech with per-host schedule state.

probes: What tables or records do you need for URLs, hosts, and seen checks?
Where does raw HTML live versus crawl metadata?

hints.1: You need URL state, host politeness/robots, and seen-sets separate from blobs.
hints.2: Sketch Url + Host + SeenUrl/SeenContent + object-store keys + frontier store.
hints.3: Url with status/depth/priority/blob keys; Host with robots/crawl_delay; Bloom/DB seen; S3 keys; Redis/SQS/Kafka frontier.

phases.goal: Draw the closed seed→frontier→fetch→parse→re-enqueue loop with queued stages and clear system boundary.

must_hit.point: Closed loop: seed URLs → URL frontier → DNS → fetch HTML → optional content-seen → parse text+links → URL filter/canonicalize → URL-seen → re-enqueue survivors; output is blob store + metadata.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Draws the full closed crawl loop ending in blobs/metadata, not a search UI.

must_hit.point: URL frontier balances priority with politeness via Mercator-style front queues (priority) and back queues per host (or host-hash); scheduler releases next URL when host delay allows (~1 in-flight request/host + crawl-delay).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names two-tier frontier and per-host release with delay / ~1 in-flight.

must_hit.point: Pipeline fetch vs parse with queues between stages; put IDs/blob keys on the queue, not raw HTML; fetcher writes object storage then enqueues parse.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Splits fetch/parse, queues blob keys, fetch writes object store then parse queue.

must_hit.point: Optional continuous mode: re-crawl scheduler scans next_fetch_at and re-enqueues; shard by hostname so politeness stays local.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions next_fetch_at scheduler and host-hash frontier shards.

probes: Draw the high-level components and the closed crawl loop.
How does the frontier enforce both priority and politeness?

hints.1: Start from seeds and follow one URL through fetch, store, parse, and re-enqueue.
hints.2: Call out frontier (priority + per-host back queues), fetcher, parser, queues, blob store.
hints.3: Seed injector → Mercator frontier → fetcher (DNS/robots/GET/blob) → parse queue → parser (links/seen) → frontier; optional re-crawl scheduler.

phases.goal: Defend 2–3 tradeoffs: politeness vs throughput, frontier design, Bloom vs exact seen, pipeline vs monolith.

must_hit.point: Politeness vs throughput: stricter per-host delay protects sites/avoids bans but stretches wall-clock; win by parallelizing across hosts, not raising per-host QPS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Argues host parallelism as the lever, not higher per-host rate.

must_hit.point: Two-tier Mercator frontier localizes politeness; single priority queue + Redis host locks is simpler ops but hotter coordination — name both.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares Mercator queues vs shared queue + host locks.

must_hit.point: Bloom vs exact DB for URL-seen: Bloom is tiny memory with false positives that skip some new URLs (usually OK); exact store has no false skip but is heavier.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States FP-only Bloom tradeoff vs exact store cost.

must_hit.point: Pipelined fetch/parse isolates I/O failures and allows re-parse without re-fetch vs monolithic crawler with fewer moving parts.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts pipeline retry/reparse benefits with monolith simplicity.

must_hit.point: BFS is simple; production mixes importance (PageRank-like / seed distance) + freshness deficit; host-hash sharding makes local politeness = global politeness with approximate cross-shard priority.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts BFS vs priority+freshness and notes sharding priority approximation.

probes: How do you keep the crawler polite without killing throughput?
Bloom filter or exact store for URL-seen — which and why?

hints.1: Pick two tradeoffs from frontier, seen-set, and fetch/parse split.
hints.2: For each: name both options, cost of each, and what you’d ship in an interview design.
hints.3: Prefer Mercator two-tier + Bloom URL-seen + pipelined fetch/parse; scale via many hosts, not higher per-host QPS.

phases.goal: Identify DNS, frontier hotspots, fetch/parse lag, dedup size, bandwidth/sockets, and crawler traps — and how to scale each.

must_hit.point: DNS is a real bottleneck at high QPS: cache resolutions aggressively and/or use multi-provider/custom resolver; don’t block the fleet on uncached lookups.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls DNS a bottleneck and answers with caching / multi-provider / custom resolver.

must_hit.point: Frontier hotspot: shard by host and keep per-host state with the shard owner so politeness stays local.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shards frontier by hostname with owner-local per-host state.

must_hit.point: Fetcher failures: retries with exponential backoff + jitter, DLQ, don’t block other hosts; parser lag: autoscale off queue depth, HTML stays in blob store.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates flaky-host retry/DLQ from parser autoscaling on queue depth.

must_hit.point: Traps/spam: max hop depth, per-host page budget, URL pattern filters/regex denylist, timeouts; also bandwidth/sockets via high concurrency, pooling, timeouts, max page size guards.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists depth/budget/pattern/timeouts plus connection/page-size guards.

probes: What bottlenecks show up first at scale, and how do you address them?
How do you handle crawler traps and flaky hosts?

hints.1: Think DNS, frontier contention, fetch vs parse imbalance, and traps.
hints.2: For each bottleneck: cache/shard/retry/autoscale/cap — map one fix.
hints.3: DNS cache; host-sharded frontier; backoff+DLQ; parser autoscaling on blobs; depth/budget/denylist.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Stricter per-host delay protects sites and avoids bans but stretches wall-clock; achieve high global throughput by crawling many hosts in parallel, not by raising per-host QPS.

tradeoffs.topic: Two-tier Mercator frontier vs single priority queue + Redis host locks
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Mercator front (priority) + back (per-host) queues localize politeness; shared queue + host locks is simpler operationally but creates hotter coordination — name both.

tradeoffs.topic: Bloom vs exact DB for URL-seen
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Bloom uses tiny memory with false positives that may skip some never-seen URLs (usually acceptable); exact DB avoids false skips but is heavier. Same idea for content-seen.
Pipeline isolates I/O failures and lets you re-parse without re-fetch, at the cost of more moving parts; monolith is simpler.
BFS is simple; production mixes importance (PageRank-like / seed distance) with freshness deficit.

tradeoffs.topic: Host-hash sharding locality vs cross-shard priority
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Sharding by hostname keeps politeness local (local = global for a host); cross-shard priority is approximate unless you add coordination.

gotchas.trap: Enforcing global politeness across many fetcher machines by letting any worker hit any host.
gotchas.correction: Shard the frontier by hostname (or use a distributed per-host lock); never let two shards own the same host.

gotchas.trap: Assuming URL-seen alone prevents duplicate work.
gotchas.correction: Same article on two hosts needs content hash / SimHash as well as URL canonicalization + URL-seen.

gotchas.trap: Treating a simple HTML GET as enough for JS-heavy SPAs.
gotchas.correction: HTML fetch can miss body content; headless browser path is expensive and usually out of scope unless asked.

gotchas.trap: Fixed weekly re-crawl for all pages in a continuous crawler.
gotchas.correction: Use adaptive next_fetch_at from observed change rate and importance (news more often than static docs).

gotchas.trap: Looking for a public product API as the center of the design.
gotchas.correction: Clarify it’s a data pipeline; seeds/status are control-plane only.

gotchas.trap: Inventing Googlebot-specific robots myths or ignoring Crawl-delay nuances.
gotchas.correction: Stick to robots.txt Disallow plus courtesy Crawl-delay; cache robots.txt per host; don’t invent bot-specific folklore.

gotchas.trap: Misstating Bloom filter error modes for URL-seen.
gotchas.correction: False positive means you skip a never-seen URL (completeness tradeoff); false negatives don’t happen on membership.

gotchas.trap: Dragging indexing, ranking, or PageRank into the crawler design unprompted.
gotchas.correction: Those are a separate system consuming your store — park unless the interviewer pulls you there.
